tone_statements.citation: Otero, Manuel Alejandro. 2019. A Historical Reconstruction of the Koman Language Family. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon (hdl.handle.net/1794/25239). Sec. 2.1.8 'Dana', printed pp. 85-93 (pp. 108-116).
tone_statements.quote: Dana displays three contrastive tone levels (L, M, H) as well as a falling (F) contour tone on a single vowel nucleus. Evidence for the tonal contrast is seen in (31). ... Tone plays an important role in the verb system. Dana employs tonal alternations on verb roots and stems to mark nominal number of participants as well as verbal number, or pluractionality (cf. Newman 1990). The general pattern for monosyllabic verb roots is seen in (32). Most common is the alternation between L and H. The M/H and F/LH alternations are less frequent in the database overall.
tone_statements.locator: Sec. 2.1.8.4 'Dana tone', pp. 92-93; summary restated in sec. 4.9, p. 265 ('Dana synchronically exhibits three contrastive level tones as well as rising and falling contour tones.. In Dana, there are no consonant-tone restrictions synchronically.')
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (Low, Mid, High) plus contour tones (falling on a single vowel nucleus, p. 92; rising and falling per the p. 265 summary); minimal quadruplet on one syllable given in (31); all three levels occur after all consonant onsets (no depressor/consonant-tone restriction, an innovation relative to Proto-Dana-Opo); grammatical tone: verb-root tonal alternations SG L ~ PL H (most common),…

tone.summary: Three level tones (Low, Mid, High) plus contour tones (falling on a single vowel nucleus, p. 92; rising and falling per the p. 265 summary); minimal quadruplet on one syllable given in (31); all three levels occur after all consonant onsets (no depressor/consonant-tone restriction, an innovation relative to Proto-Dana-Opo); grammatical tone: verb-root tonal alternations SG L ~ PL H (most common),…
tone.says: Dana has three contrastive level tones L, M, H plus a falling contour on a single vowel nucleus (p. 92; p. 265 adds rising and falling contours and states there are no consonant-tone restrictions synchronically); tone is heavily grammatical in the verb: tonal alternations on roots/stems mark participant number and pluractionality, mostly L~H, less often M/H and F/LH (p. 93). No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the work.
